That opening sequence is fantastic. The whole one-shot concept grabbed me immediately, and the cinematography is incredible. But who really wants to sit through almost two hours of World War I? After the initial wow factor wore off, this became a bit of a snooze fest for me. Beautifully made, technically impressive, great performances—but watching two guys slog through trenches, mud, explosions and misery for two hours just wasn’t doing it for me. Maybe if I’d grown up hearing World War I stories from my grandparents or great-grandparents, or if there were a couple of major stars carrying me through it, I’d feel differently. But it’s a bunch of characters I have no connection to, fighting a war that feels increasingly distant. At this point, historical war dramas like this feel less like entertainment and more like an Ambien.

Not a fan. It felt like a theme park ride. Specifically one of those dark rides at an amusement park. You're just moved from one set piece to another with a thin objective as to why you're being moved around. The whole movie felt like it was on a rail. I couldn't get past that, and given how predictable the events of the movie are, it wasn't an exciting ride. I felt it mostly had to do with the continuous take mechanism. Its the dominating trait of the movie, and much like Rope, its an impressive process and the cuts are cleverly hidden. I can't imagine how many things had to go right for the end product to look this seamless. And to see the camera somehow keep up no matter what scene its in was cool. It's great cinematography, it shined the most in the burning village halfway into the movie. And the technical work behind the movie is still impressive: the expansive & detailed sets, as well as the huge number of extras (epic in scale, but for a simple 1hr50 movie!). But beyond that, I couldn't find anything noteworthy about the movie. Once you see what the movie is trying to do with the continuous take, it quickly wears off and becomes a gimmick, and then starts actively drawing attention to itself, almost like it's to distract from how thin the story actually is and how lacking it is in substance. I cannot name one notable thing that happened in the first hour - actually, in the entire movie - anything that makes me want to rewatch it. Put aside the continuous shot gimmick and there's just not much left to the movie itself. Even the climatic run during the attack, and the ending itself were both really underwhelming. The dialogue was dull, the emotional moments were predictable and manipulative, the bad guys were just cartoonishly evil obstacles, the sound design was drowned out by the score, I eventually couldn't wait for the whole thing to end. It felt like the movie has no substance beyond its continuous shot style. Overall, it was really underwhelming.

I saw this film on its first release in 2020 and I see from my history gave it 2.5 stars (indifferent/ mediocre). It’s one of the films where I find myself quite a bit out of step with the Letterboxd consensus, so I eventually got round to a re-watch to find out what I was missing. I have decided to revisit my mark - by knocking 1/2 mark off (2 stars = bad but not awful, so it has a redeeming feature). Given that there are many others who love this movie (and I appreciate that some of those have actually war experience and so cannot be dismissed), let me try to explain. Technically, this film is outstanding. The cinematography by the great Roger Deakins, the editing by Lee Smith, the lighting and the sound design - all beyond reproach. They all contribute to the apparent single shot presentation which is, at least as a technical achievement, rightly much lauded. At least in the first act and toward the end of the third this presentation drew me in and made the film seem immersive. But for me that is where it ends. This is a film that almost screams “Look how brilliant the director/ cinematographer/ sound is” in every moment at the cost of everything else. The plot is thin, contains far too many unlikely coincidences and events requiring a total suspension of belief. In particular there is a scene with a French woman and child that is tacky and adds nothing to the plot or action. The plot also drags a bit in places and it really needed to be faster paced. There are some fine cameos, particularly by Andrew Scott, Mark Strong and Benedict Cumberbatch, but the leads are ill-served by the script. This is a world populated by stereotypes - the Germans are all (very) bad,  the serving man the suffering salt of the earth. Beyond that there is no characterisation to speak of, and the lead character(s) are uncharismatic and totally emotionless. By the end of the film, I didn’t care what happened to anyone. There are of course other one shot presentation films - Birdman and Rope spring to mind - but none on the scale of this. For that reason, I suspect that 1917 might be on the syllabus of film courses for years to come. If I had been marking this film solely on technical achievement, certainly a 4.5, possibly a 5. But for the casual viewer, this is basically a gimmick film that is all about spectacle and special effects - more of an experience than a narrative film and you may find your attention wandering long before the end. While I admire the craft, I cannot recommend it to other than film students.

Beyond the technical achievements of the film, much of the experience is bogged down by pacing issues and shallow dramaturgy, thoroughly reliant on a flimsy emotional stake that simply never stuck deep enough to elevate the otherwise amazing set pieces. Formally, too, there's almost no reason to invest any interest, as it never really moves past the gimmick of a oner, nor does it have the balls to fully commit to the bit. The camera wanders around and swings past our characters, but it feels more like a cam op hitting their marks rather than a fleshed out visual direction; it simply stages the next set-piece for us to see. The only time that the camera does feel like an actual cinematic instrument was in the trenches, where the claustrophobic corridors and shifting uniformed bodies serve to juxtapose the movements our characters are making; opposite against the huddled safety of the masses, away from the high walls of the trenches, into the open air of death. C'est un bordel sans nom où tout peut dépendre du sprint d'une seule personne et du courant de la rivière. Le seul bémol, c'est les personnages principaux. Je ne me suis pas vraiment attaché à eux. À partir de ce là, c'est très très dur de ressentir des émotions humaines. On se limite aux émotions cinématographiques : la tension, l'inspiration, l'admiration... I feel like i'm probably going to get attacked for only giving this 3 stars because this movie is INSANELY WELL MADE, but i just didn't connect with it as much as i thought i would. The biggest thing about 1917 is obviously the one-shot style, and yeah, it's fucking impressive. The way the camera follows Schofield and Blake through the trenches, fields and destroyed villages makes you feel like you're actually waling through WW1 with them. There were definitely moments where i completely forgot about the camera and just got sucked into what was happening. And visually, this movie is ridiculous. Roger Deakins absolutely cooked. The lighting, the landscapes, the trenches, the burning buildings at night - there are so many shots where i was just thinking  "how did they even film this?" The opening section with Schofield and Blake was probably my favourite. Their friendship feels natural, and i actually cared about what happened to them. George MacKay is also really good, especially as the movie gets more intense and Schofield is basically running on fear and adrenaline. But i think that's where my problem is. I admired the filmmaking way more than i connected with the actual story. The "one continuous shot" idea is amazing technically, but sometimes it felt like the gimmick was more interesting to me than the characters. There are also quite a few moments where i could almost see the movie setting up the next impressive shot or sequence. The film is definitely at it's best when it slows down and lets you actually sit with what's happening. The scenes where Schofield is just walking through the aftermath of everything are honestly more affecting to me than some of the bigger action sequences. It makes war feel less like an epic story and more like a horrible, exhausting place that these young men have been thrown into. The final stretch was probably the closest i got to being completely invested. Watching Schofield desperately trying to to reach the soldiers while everything is falling apart around him had me properly stressed. Incredible cinematography, great performances, amazing atmosphere, but i was more impressed than emotionally destroyed. 3/5

Sam Mendes — THE FORMALIST!! Sam Mendes continues to walk in Christopher Nolan's shadow when it comes to his big-budget films. It was clear in Skyfall and clear in Spectre . These are films that want to be more than just action and adventure. It might sound harsh, but he wears his influences openly. He wants to make big films that are also important films! Much has been said about the choice to make the film appear as if shot in a single take, and yes, it largely works — because every department is striving for perfection. Otherwise, it's easy for long takes to become an exercise in "good enough," so as to avoid having to redo them. But here, the tension is maintained more or less throughout. It's difficult to speculate how the film would have played conventionally edited, because it would have needed an entirely different story — as it now hinges entirely on unfolding in real time, with no room for deeper dives into either characters or themes. So it's fairly pointless to entertain that thought experiment. The main thing is that the stylistic choice has been made, it's followed through, and it makes the film feel more significant than it might otherwise have been. The story doesn’t come with any sort of surprises whatsoever. It is only novel in the way it is told. Form and story in symbiosis. The problem I have is that it becomes so controlled — the sense of danger rarely comes through as clearly as it could. When it works, it works, but it comes a little too rarely, since we are constantly being pushed forward and forward.

For *1917*, I think the obvious thing that fits your taste is the **cinematography and the illusion that you're following them in one continuous shot**. But I would not make it purely technical because the friendship and urgency of the mission are what give that filmmaking weight. 1917 is one of those films where the way it was made is almost as impressive as the story itself. The decision to make the film appear as one continuous shot is incredible. Rather than watching the war from a distance, the camera follows Blake and Schofield through everything. Across trenches, through fields, into abandoned buildings and eventually straight into battle. There’s rarely an opportunity to escape from what they’re experiencing, and that makes the whole mission feel much more intense. Roger Deakins’ cinematography is absolutely stunning. There are so many shots where I find myself thinking about how they actually managed to capture them, especially knowing how precisely the actors, camera crew, sets and effects had to work together to maintain the illusion of one continuous journey. The nighttime sequence through Écoust with the flares lighting the ruins is probably one of the best-looking sequences in the entire film. What really makes it work though is that all of that technical brilliance actually serves the story. The mission itself is incredibly simple: cross enemy territory and deliver a message that could save 1,600 men. Because you stay with Blake and Schofield for almost every step, you start feeling the distance, exhaustion and constant danger alongside them. The friendship between them gives it the emotional weight it needs too. What begins as two soldiers carrying out an order gradually becomes something much more personal, and there are moments that hit incredibly hard without the film needing to overdo them. I also love how the war is portrayed. It isn’t constantly trying to give you huge battles. Some of the most tense moments come from silence, empty trenches or simply not knowing what might be around the next corner. Then when the film does open up into something bigger, it feels enormous. And that final run across the battlefield while everyone else charges in the opposite direction is one of those scenes I could watch again and again. Brilliant cinematography, incredible attention to detail and a simple story made unbelievably intense by how it was filmed. Definitely one that made me appreciate just how much work can go into getting a shot exactly right.

Having watched Birdman before, the simulated continual shot was a style of interest to me and 1917 definitely delivered with its two shot style. Not only does 1917 pull this off smoothly, but with great narrative effect. What 1917 has to offer is a visual production and cinematography behemoth, earning its Oscars' multiple times over. This should come as no surprise from director Sean Mendes, whose work on Spectre (2015) and Skyfall (2012) share the larger-than-life visual style of Mendes, with Spectre including a long duration tracking shot commonplace in 1917. 1917 shows no qualms with the brutality on display that defined WWI and tells no lies in the unceremonious slaughter of millions. The reality of the matter is the trenches and the space between them were simply hell on earth. 1917 leverages its transition to the second continual shot to further drive home this hellscape. Likely in homage to The Iliad and Greek mythology at large, we cross the river and are shot in head and black out. We awake to a world in ruin, a dark, destroyed landscape lit only by towering fire and flash of guns. What I believe Mendes shows here is in tribute to the crossing of the River Styx into the land of the dead, and we stay in this hellscape until we cross the river once more to return to the land of the living. Cinematically, the time spent inbetween river crossings is some of the most visually stunning, emotionally evocative pieces that I have ever seen. That experience alone is worth seeing this film. While there are many things to praise about this film, to avoid being long-winded I'll keep it to this. 1917 is more than deserving of its accolades and is a flexing of Mendes' cinematic vision that pays off in a big way. Undoubtably worth your time. 8.5/10

Breathtaking, stunning, immersive cinematic masterpiece that showcases the horrors of World War I into a ticking clock survival thriller. Director Sam Mendes successfully strips away the typical political grandiosity of historical war epics to focus on a intimate, terrifyingly immediate human story of loyalty and perseverance. The film’s best element is that it is crafted to appear as one continuous, unbroken tracking shot unfolding in real time. Legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins uses clever camera movements, hidden cuts, and brilliant staging to pull the audience into the trenches alongside the soldiers. It removes the detachment of traditional editing, making you feel less like a viewer and more like a third runner on the mission. Early in the film, Blake points out chopped down cherry trees, noting that the scattered seeds will still grow back. Later, when Schofield is floating down a river choked with dead bodies, white cherry blossoms gently fall from the sky. It symbolizes that life and beauty will eventually outlast the cruelty of war. The ending beautifully captures that while the physical war continues unabated, Schofield has undergone a profound internal shift. Through Blake’s sacrifice, he moves from being a numb, detached survivor to a man who fully understands the value of human dignity and emotional connection. George MacKay and Dean Charles Chapman carries the film entirely on their shoulders. As the camera rarely leaves them, their performances required immense physical and emotional endurance. Both delivered a remarkably grounded and physical performance. With a script that intentionally lacks heavy dialogue or prolonged exposition dumps, MacKay and Chapman had to communicate raw vulnerability, fear, and sheer adrenaline through their facial expressions and body language. MacKay in particular, received significant praise for carrying the emotional weight of the film's second half. His ability to portray a quiet, desperate resilience that keeps the audience invested in the human drama amidst the chaotic spectacle of war. Overall 1917 is a breathtaking achievement that demands the biggest screen possible. Even if the narrative path is straightforward, the sheer scale of craftsmanship makes it an unforgettable, heart pounding journey.

Quite simply, 1917 is a masterpiece. World War I and its history are almost always diminished in comparison to the Second World War. But if there were one war in history I would never, ever volunteer to fight in, it would be this one. This was the war in which warfare truly became modern. Thousands of years of romanticized notions of glory, ego, pride, and honor were stripped away in the mud and trenches—at the cost of millions of lives. Millions of young lives. And 1917 illustrates the idiocy of it all: why war, despite sometimes being unavoidable, is such an extraordinary waste of human life, potential, and beauty. Not only are the main characters masterfully portrayed, but the filmmaking itself is astonishing. The movie is constructed to feel like one nearly continuous journey, with extraordinarily long takes and seamless transitions that rarely allow the audience a moment to escape. The emotion and tension remain almost constant. You don’t simply watch these men cross the battlefield—you feel as though you are walking beside them. You feel trapped in the mud, the ruins, the trenches, and the chaos with them. That immersion is what makes the film so powerful. Beneath the spectacle is something deeply human: young men trying to survive, trying to fulfill their duty, and trying to save one another in the middle of something unimaginably destructive. I think everyone should watch this film. Despite its R rating, I believe it is an important illustration of what war actually costs. I’m grateful films like 1917 exist—not to glorify war, but to preserve the memory of those who endured it and to remind us why we should never forget.
